body_markdown:
As Ford speeds toward a tech-filled future with its universal EV production system, expanded BlueCruise capabilities, and a potential overall win at Le Mans in a fancy new Hypercar, the company is clearly keeping one foot in the past, as evident by the contents of a 79,000-square-foot building in Romulus, Michigan.


The lobby is filled with old posters, memorabilia, and a pale-yellow antique kitchenette, and it only hints at the incredible collection of relics beyond a pair of blue doors by the back wall. Step past the threshold, and you’re transported into a time capsule that envelopes the Blue Oval’s 125-year history. This is the Ford Vault.


You might have heard the story by now. This heritage project has been in the works for a while, and we even covered the announcement last year when[Grace Jarvis reported on its launch](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/8-notable-vehicles-from-fords-new-u-s-heritage-collection/) . According to the lore, when Ford CEO Jim Farley saw what his U.K. counterparts were doing at the Daventry Innovation Center, he suggested to his American team that they needed their own heritage fleet. Ford’s head archivist, Ted Ryan, got to work assembling a collection of meaningful rides. Now, they have an official home.


The Ford Vault is just a stone’s throw outside of Detroit. This ex-Amazon warehouse underwent a massive transformation as Ford moved in, bringing with it some 125 historic vehicles. The company wishes to make its collection “accessible to the people building Ford’s future,” from employees to community members, and the end result is a roster of vehicles that could rival any museum.

The building is immaculate, with newly finished floors and proper lighting (check out the photos). Unlike[The Henry Ford](https://www.thehenryford.org/) (arguably the most prominent Ford museum, and about 30 minutes down the street), there are minimal stands and velvet ropes. If you’re not careful, you may literally rub elbows with giants.


Of course, the facility is still evolving. As Ford puts it: “The space is just coming to life—the paint is still drying as the final touches are added.” No matter, we visited the place last week for the cars, and boy, were there plenty. Concepts, test mules, celebrity rides, milestone cars, and even a few vehicles that many thought were lost to time. Let’s talk about several of our favorites, then you can scroll through the rest.


## **2005 Mustang GT — 2015 GT350 Prototype**


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


Meet Johnny Cash. Engineers named this experimental Mustang after the country music star because the car was built “one piece at a time.” The pony started life as a garden-variety 2005 Mustang GT before it became an early prototype in the 2007 Cobra program. This program was eventually paused for the Ford GT program.


“This is a really unique car,” says Nick Terzes, Ford Racing’s heritage business manager. “Everybody walks by it, and I can see why.” Those in the know might spot its rollcage, which was installed to test an experimental independent rear suspension, or spy something fishy in the engine compartment. Early on in Ford’s testing of flat-plane cranks, they lowered a 4.6-liter flat-plane crank prototype engine between the red fenders of this GT. The car also features a 2013 GT500 transmission and driveshaft and served as a 2015 GT350 prototype. “It has led a very abused life, but it’s one that we saved,” says Terzes.


## **1998 Stewart SF02 Formula 1**


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


In case you’ve been living under a rock,[Ford is back in F1](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/red-bull-and-racing-bulls-unveil-a-new-look-for-the-2026-f1-season/) . This year, they supplied a bespoke powertrain to Red Bull Racing. This Stewart SF02, now almost 30 years old, is a distant relative of the Red Bull program.


Stewart Grand Prix Limited, an F1 team in the late ’90s founded by Sir Jackie Stewart and his son Paul, was a Ford factory-backed effort. After just three seasons, Ford bought the team outright, and it became Jaguar Racing. Then, in 2004, Jaguar Racing was sold to energy drink company Red Bull GmbH and was rebranded Red Bull Racing in 2005.


This SF02 features a 3.0L Zetec-R V-10 and a cool livery with tartan stripes, a reference to founder Jackie Stewart’s Scottish roots.


## **2016 Ford GT Powertrain Mule**


[Cameron Neveu](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/cameron-neveu/)


The well-chronicled development path of Ford’s second-generation GT (and its run at modern Le Mans glory) is paved with a handful of test mules that could easily double as extras in[a Mad Max movie](https://www.hagerty.com/media/entertainment/furiosa-feeds-mad-max-franchises-lust-for-misfit-machines/) .


Terzes explains that, to keep costs down, Ford engineers only install certain parts in prototypes, reusing existing bits wherever they can. This particular example is a powertrain mule, so the car has a 3.5-liter twin-turbocharged EcoBoost V-6 under an engine cover wrapped in duct tape. An instrument cluster and steering wheel out of a Mustang, trailer taillamps, and mirrors from a snowmobile (Terzes’ best guess) drive home the “only necessary parts” mantra.

## **Ford Mustang “Ute” Concept**


> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfsQgfZvHSG/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
>
>
> [A post shared by Hagerty (@hagerty)](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfsQgfZvHSG/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)


This Mustang Ute Concept was built by Ford’s EVB Metal Shop, as a way to train apprentices by allowing them to get real-world, hands-on experience while building a concept car.


The bed floor is a production Ranger part, melded into the Mustang body. The original Mustang decklid was converted into a functional tailgate as well.
